The KERNAL's RS-232 interrupt flags; $03F4 clears it before a load so no serial interrupt can interfere.
The KERNAL's PAL/NTSC flag (1 on PAL), set at power-on: $0633 reads it to adjust the fast loader's timing.
The KERNAL's IRQ vector; $EC95 points it at $E1AC as well as $FFFE, although the game runs with the KERNAL banked out.
The high byte of the KERNAL's IRQ vector, set to $E1 by $EC9D.
The game's first instruction, where the title program's JMP $03C0 hands over: one jump to the start-up at $EC66. GAM0 loads from $03C0, so this is also the first byte of that file.

Loads one file from drive 8 with the game's own fast loader. Filename at ($BB) with its length in $B7, load address in X (low) and Y (high), or the file's own address when $02 says so. A name starting with "$" goes to $248D instead. Masks the raster interrupt and CIA 1's, banks the KERNAL in ($01=$36) for the drive commands, blanks the screen ($D011=$0B), calls $0504, then banks back to $35 and turns the raster interrupt on again.
A filename beginning "$" (the directory) is not loaded: it jumps to $248D.

238 bytes of 1541 drive code. $0504 writes 256 bytes from here into the drive's RAM at $0600-$06FF with M-W commands and starts it with M-E at $06C7 (so its entry is $04DD here); the last 18 bytes it sends are the start of $0504 itself, sent along and not run. The drive finds the file and sends it two bits at a time over the serial port, which $0621 reads.

Opens the file through the KERNAL (OPEN, TALK, TKSA, ACPTR, CLOSE) to make the drive find it, and returns if the status $90 says it failed. Then uploads the drive code at $0416 in eight 32-byte M-W blocks, starts it with M-E, and receives the file: each block begins with a count byte, the first block's next two bytes are the load address (kept, or replaced by X/Y from $03C3), and every data byte is stored through $0665 with all ROMs and I/O banked out. Returns the end address in X/Y.
"M-W" and "M-E" followed by $C7 $06: the drive commands $0504 sends; the M-E jumps to $06C7 in the drive.
The file was found: uploads the drive code ($0416, 32 bytes a time with M-W to drive $0600-$06FF), starts it with M-E, then receives the file block by block until the drive sends a short block.
Reads the two bytes of a block's load address from the drive into $AE/$AF (and $C6/$C7); when $02 is zero, $AE/$AF take the caller's address from $C3/$C4 instead.

Receives one byte from the drive: signals ready on CIA 2 port A ($DD00=$0B), waits for the drive to pull bit 7, then reads $DD00 four times, two bits each (bits 6 and 7), building the byte in $A4. Flashes the border down and up around each byte, which is the stripe pattern seen while it loads. The two BEQs on $02A6 (the KERNAL's PAL/NTSC flag) branch to the next instruction either way: they adjust the timing by a cycle on PAL machines.
Stores A at ($AE),Y with $01=$30 (all RAM, no I/O), so a file can load under the I/O area and the ROMs, then restores $01=$36 and steps Y.

Expands the level's tile map into the character map the screen scrolls over: 144 tile columns ($190F counts them) of 35 tiles each, read down a column from ($3E/$3F), which steps 64 bytes a column. Each map byte names a 2x2 tile, whose four characters it reads from $4000 + byte*4 and writes as two rows of two into a map 288 characters wide starting at $7D80, so the level is 288 by 70 characters ($7D80-$CC3F). When $1AAE is $10 it then puts character $47 into sixteen cells, four rows of four from $A028.
A lone RTS: the handler for behaviours and pickups that do nothing, named in several tables ($077D, $10CE, $178F).
"TITLE", the file $0766 loads when the game is over. No file of that name is on this disk (its title program is called LOADER).

The game is over: loads "TITLE" at $C000 and jumps there. On this disk image there is no file called TITLE, so the load finds nothing and the jump runs the level data that is at $C000, which crashes (facts.md).

27 words, one per behaviour number (even numbers $00-$34, kept in $B2+slot), each the routine $0F70 calls for an object every pass by writing it into the JSR at $0FA6. $00-$10 are $0F61 (animate only); then $0D81, $0D91, $09D5, $09D9, $085B, $EA16, $28A5, $28B3, $28D0, $0BFD, $0DDD, $0B27, $0A05, $08E6, $0899, $07B3, $EAD4 and $0760.
The high bytes of behaviour_handlers's two-byte entries, which $0F82 reads through $077E, indexed.

Behaviour $30: an enemy that hides and shows itself. With frame 0 it sets frame $E7, a countdown of $1E in its record and a position, or empties itself; while shown it counts the record's +$0B down to frame $E1 and moves one pixel left a pass. When the player stands on its 8-line row and its countdown at +$0C has run out, it fires into slot 1 (if free) with sound $10.

Behaviour $1A: a thrown object that climbs 3 lines a pass while the counter $28A2 runs down, switching to frame $AC with sound $0D when it reaches $13, and removes itself at line $B8 or when the counter runs out.

Behaviour $2E: counts its record's +$0B down, showing frame $A7 below $46; at the end of the count it waits a random $50-$6F passes and, when slot 0 is free, puts a copy of itself into slot 0 as behaviour $1A with frame $AA and sets $28A2 (to $30, or $26 when $1AAE is below 2).

Behaviour $2C: waits a random 0-127 passes, then if the player is on its 8-line row turns to face him (frames $AD and $A9) and fires into slot 0 or 1 (a random wait of $64-$83 if both are busy); on another row it shows frame $A5 and, when it and the player are on the same side and slot 0 is free, throws itself into slot 0 as behaviour $1A with sound $0E.
Scratch: bit 7 of the enemy's x for the comparison at $0944.
Fires into slot Y: places the shot 12 pixels left of the enemy (24 right when it faces right), gives it behaviour $12 or $14 by slot, frame $AB or $AF, and sets the direction flag $0EE6,Y.
Behaviour $16, slot 0's dropped object (and $09D9, behaviour $18, slot 1's): falls 4 lines a pass for the count in $0A85,Y, then ends its frame; on the count's last turn it empties the slot.
Behaviour $18: slot 1's falling object, sharing $09DB with $09D5.

Behaviour $2A: an enemy that walks back and forth (the walking at $0A96) and, when the player is below it and a projectile slot is free, drops an object into it (behaviour $16 or $18, frame $CF, fall count $0F) with sound $0E, showing frames $B5/$C3 while doing so.
Starts slot Y's falling object 16 lines below the enemy, with behaviour $16 or $18, a fall count of 15 and frame $CF, and plays sound $0E on voice 2.
Two counters, for slots 0 and 1: how many more passes their dropped object falls.
The player is above the enemy: no drop. Shows the walking frame $B5, or $C3 when its record's byte $0D says it faces the other way.

Behaviour $28: an enemy that turns to face the player (frames $D1 and $D9) and, at a random interval of 0-7 passes, fires into slot 0 or 1 when the player is on its 8-line row (frames $DE/$D6 for the shot, $D3/$DB for itself) with sound $0C on voice 2.

Behaviour $24: an object that moves in an arc, 2 pixels sideways a pass (the way its record's +$0D says) and up or down by the next step of the table at $0CE1; a frame $F7 one that goes below line $A1, or any that reaches $B6, is removed by $0CD2. While a frame $F7 one is still above that line it clears $28A4, sets $0CD1, and keeps a second object (frame $F2 or the next frame) 21 lines below it in the next slot.
Set to 1 by $0BFD while a frame $F7 object is in the air; the player's update at $1018 does nothing while it is set, and $1F37 and $E012 read it too.
Removes the arcing object (and, for frame $F7, the one below it).

80 two-byte steps of an arc for $0BFD, of which only the low byte is added to the object's line: -4 three times, -2 three times, -1 four times, 0 twice, then +4 to the end. The high bytes ($FF for the negative steps, $00 otherwise) are not read.

Behaviour $12, a shot in slot 0: animates and flies 3 pixels a pass left or right by the flag at $0EE6, and empties the slot when it leaves the screen ($0DA1, $0DBF). $0D91, behaviour $14, is the same for slot 1 with the flag at $0EE7.
Behaviour $14: slot 1's shot, as $0D81 with the direction flag $0EE7.
Moves a shot 3 pixels left and empties its slot once it is left of x $14.
Moves a shot 3 pixels right and empties its slot once it is past x $138.

Behaviour $26: an enemy that patrols (the walk at $0E55, with a random pause of $10-$2F) and, when the player is on its 8-line row and past x $1E, fires into slot 0 or 1 through $0EE8; frames $B5/$C3 while walking and $B9/$C7 standing.
Unused: nothing calls or jumps here. Turns frame $B9 into $B5, or $C7 into $C3, the standing frames of the patrolling enemy into its walking ones.
Two flags, for slots 0 and 1: $FF when the shot flies left, 0 when it flies right.
Slot 1's shot direction, the second byte of $0EE6: $FF when it flies left.

Fires into slot Y with sound $0C on voice 1: faces the shooter toward the player (frames $C5/$B7), places the shot 12 pixels left of it (+24 when it flies right), with frame $CF or $C1, and sets behaviour $12/$14.

Steps an object's animation: adds to its frame number ($D2+X) the value the level's table at $387B gives for that frame, so each frame names the next. Skipped while $0FB9 is not zero, so objects animate on one pass in three.

Runs every object's behaviour, slots 12 down to 0: a slot whose line ($E2+X) is zero, or whose behaviour ($B2+X) is zero or negative, is skipped. The behaviour's routine comes from $077D and is written into the JSR at $0FA6; for behaviours from $24 on it first points $13/$14 at the enemy's record (from $E82E by $63+X) and copies the record's byte 7 into $C2+X, inverted when $C2+X was negative so that its bit 7 is kept. Then counts $0FB9 down from 2.
The low byte of the operand of the JSR at $0FA6, rewritten by $0F7F before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the JSR at $0FA6, rewritten by $0F85 before it runs.
Counts 2, 1, 0 across passes; $0F61 only steps frames when it is 0.
Copies a zero-terminated string from ($21) to ($13) as screen codes: letters ($40 and up) less $40, digits less $30, anything else becomes 0 (a space in the panel's set).
Unused: nothing calls or jumps here. Counts the record's byte $0E and moves the object one pixel left or right by it, then runs on into $1000; the patrol of an enemy type the game no longer has.

Counts a record's timer at ($13),Y down by one; when it runs out, reloads it from the next byte and flips the direction byte at +$0E. Only the self-modified JSR at $10C4 names this address: that JSR's operand is replaced before every call, so this routine is the operand left in the file and is never called through it.

Checks the player against every other object once a pass, unless the arc flag $0CD1 or the dying flag $1123 is set. Walks the multiplexer's sorted list at $7F-$8E (read as $FF8F,X with X from $F0 to $FF, an address that wraps past $FFFF) to the objects whose line lies between $5D and $7A, skips objects 0-2, and keeps those within $2D pixels to the right of the player's x less $19 on the same side of x 256. An object with type 0 ($AF+n) is an enemy: touching it hurts through $11FD, unless the player is already hurt this pass ($127F), while $E6C7 is set, or in the middle of a move ($369F between 1 and $1D). Any other type is a pickup or hazard, whose routine $10CE names and $10C4 calls.
The low byte of the operand of the CMP at $1056, rewritten by $1045 before it runs.
The low byte of the operand of the CMP at $106B, rewritten by $104B before it runs.
The low byte of the operand of the JSR at $10C4, rewritten by $10BB before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the JSR at $10C4, rewritten by $10C1 before it runs.
27 words by object type ($AF+n, even): what touching an object does. Type 2 $116E, 4 $11B8, 6 $1151, 8 $1194, $0A $11E1, $12-$22 $1105 (a hazard); the rest $0760, nothing.
The high bytes of contact_handlers's two-byte entries, which $10BE reads through $10CF, indexed.
Passes left in which a hazard ($1105) cannot hurt again: set to $B4 (180) on each hit; counted down at $3678.

Type $12-$22, a hazard: removes the object and, unless $1104 is still counting, takes 10 from the energy $F373, redraws the bar and starts the 180-pass cooldown. Energy that would go below zero makes the player die instead ($1124).
1 while the player is dying: set by $1124 when the energy runs out, which also stops the collision checks and the controls.
Out of energy: sets $1123 and gives the player the falling frame $62 (or $76 when $5C is 0, facing the other way).
Unused: nothing calls it. A version of the hazard at $1105 that takes 5 energy instead of 10, with the same 180-pass cooldown.
Type 6: removes the object, adds a life to $373C, redraws the lives ($F3F0) and plays sound 4.
Type 2: removes the object and adds one, in decimal, to $F359, redrawn by $F35B (the count beside the bullet icon); sound 7.
0, 3 or 6: raised by 3 at each type 8 pickup ($1194), never to 9. The player's shooting code ($1E5E onward) adds it to its frame numbers.
Type 8: removes the object and raises $1193 by 3 unless it would reach 9; sound 5.
Type 4: removes the object and adds $10 to the energy $F373, at most $40; sound 3.
Type $0A: removes the object and scores entry 0 of the table at $F202 (400 points); sound 6.

The player has walked into an enemy: sets $127F, pushes the player one pixel away from it (left when the enemy's $60+n is 1, right when 2), sets the facing byte $BF to 6 or 9 ($FFF1 decides which), puts the player $13 lines above the enemy's $DF+n, and if his animation pointer $4A/$4B is at $24F6 or $24F9 switches it to $24AA (or $24BD when $5C is 0).
Set when $11FD pushes the player back; cleared at the top of $1018 every pass.
Counted up by the interrupt at $12F4, once a frame.

Raster interrupt at the bottom of the play area: turns on extended colour mode and the 25-row screen with fine scroll 7, moves all eight sprites to 0,0 so none show over the panel, clears the horizontal fine scroll and points $D018 at the panel's characters, then sets $12F4 for line $C6.
Raster interrupt at line $C6: counts $1280 up, sets $132B for line $CA, waits 16 NOPs and sets $D011 to fine scroll 1 with extended colour off.

Raster interrupt at line $CA: after a short delay blanks the 24/25-row bits of $D011 (opening the lower border), sets the panel's two background colours ($06 blue, $0E light blue), sets $136F for line 0 and calls the sound update $F88F.

Raster interrupt at line 0: turns all sprites on, sets the level's colours from $FD99-$FD9C, the play screen's $D018 from $43, horizontal scroll from $41 and vertical scroll from $42, and sets $E1AC (the sprite interrupt) for the line in $F313.

Draws the visible window of the level from scratch onto both screens at $4000 and $4400, 18 rows of 40 characters, with each character's colour from the level's table at $FD9D into colour RAM. The map address is $7D80's row table at $170B (by the camera's y in $29/$2A, in 8-line rows) plus the camera's x in $27/$28 less $18, in 8-pixel columns. Then draws the panel: score, ammo, energy, lives and the $E915 bar.
Set to $FF with $14B5 when a life starts ($19A0); written and read by the scroll and attack code ($2575, $26FC-$2716).

The direction the screen is scrolling, twice the direction number (0 up, 2 up-right, and so on clockwise to $0E up-left), or $FF when it is still. Times 8, plus twice the fine-scroll step, it indexes the scroll tables at $178F, $188F and $28ED.
The half of the double buffer being drawn: $10 or 0, from bit 4 of $43 after $1584 flips it.
Scratch: twice the scroll step in $1529.
Twice the scroll step, kept by $1529 for the table index. The seven bytes after it are not read by the scroll code.
Paired with $14C1: per-direction steps read by $2766.
A table of 16 bytes read by $276D, one per direction and step: 0, 1 or $FF, how the camera's x moves.
Paired with $14D1: per-direction steps read by $2775.
A table of 16 bytes read by $277C, one per direction and step: 0, 1 or $FF, how the camera's y moves.

One pass of the 8-way scroller. When nothing scrolls ($14B5 negative) it just runs the objects ($0F70), the player's animation ($1A85), the timers ($3678) and the sprite sort ($F2B3). Otherwise it sets the fine scroll bytes $41 and $42 from the camera's position ($27 and $29, inverted in their low three bits), picks this pass's routine from the table at $178F by direction, buffer half and fine-scroll step, and calls it through the JSR at $1569 (each copies one slice of the screen into the hidden buffer); when the step is the one the table at $28ED marks, it flips the shown screen (bit 4 of $43) and calls the edge-drawing routine from $188F through the JSR at $1584. A $FF entry stops the scroll ($14B5=$FF, $3755).
The low byte of the operand of the JSR at $1569, rewritten by $1566 before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the JSR at $1569, rewritten by $1560 before it runs.
The low byte of the operand of the JSR at $1584, rewritten by $153E before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the JSR at $1584, rewritten by $1544 before it runs.

Works out, for the scroll direction, where the new edge comes from: the level map address of the top-left of the window ($170B row table by camera y, plus camera x less $18, in characters) into $34/$35 and $36/$37, offset by the direction's entries in $16EB and $16FB, and the screen row and column to draw into, $32 and $33, from $16DB/$16DC ($FF for none).

Runs a jump or a fall step by step. $369F is the step (even, 0 when standing); a jump starts when up is pressed (bit 3 of $F355). Reads the play area under and around the player and decides what he can do. The sprite multiplexer's raster interrupt, entered first at the line in $F313 and again lower down while objects are left. When the next object's line is at or below $44 (the line the interrupt was set for plus $22) it stops, writes the address of the sprite to continue with into the JMP at $E1B3, and sets the next interrupt 13 lines above that object ($E457). When the list ends it sets $1281 for line $BF, the panel.

Dying frames by enemy type ($26 on, two bytes each), used when the record's byte $0D is set: $C0, $D5, $C0, $B1, $A9, $EE, $F7.
Dying frames by enemy type, used otherwise: $CE, $DD, $CE, $B1, $A9, $EE, $F7.
For each scroll direction, which fine scroll decides the step: 1 (vertical, $42) for up and down, 0 (horizontal, $41) for the rest.

The main loop, once a pass: resets the stack, waits for the frame and plays the sound ($F274), checks the pause key ($E12F), runs the player ($1912) and the clock ($F424), moves the bullets ($1EB1), handles the fire button ($1DB3) and moves the walkers ($E713).
Eight masks that $ED5A ANDs into eight bytes of the character set at a time (operands written by $ED6E), from $E99E or $E9DE by the stage: the wipe between stages.
The second of the eight masks of the first wipe step, the operand $EDD0 starts with.
The third mask of the first wipe step, operand of $EDD8.
The fourth mask of the first wipe step, operand of $EDE0.
The fifth mask of the first wipe step, operand of $EDE8.
The sixth mask of the first wipe step, operand of $EDF0.
The seventh mask of the first wipe step, operand of $EDF8.
The eighth mask of the first wipe step and the rest of the first set: 64 bytes of masks in all from $E99E, each step's eight clearing more of a character's pixels.

The second set of wipe masks, used on stages whose number has bit 1 set (2, 6, $0A, $0E, $12, $16, $1A). $ED5A reads 64 bytes from here, so its last eight masks are the first bytes of the code at $EA16.
The last bytes of the second mask set that lie before $EA16.

Behaviour $1C, something that crosses the screen right to left, 2 pixels a pass on stage 0 and 4 on the others, and disappears at the left edge. On stages $10 and $1C it closes on the player's row, 4 lines a pass. On stages $16 and $1C, unless its frame is $A4, it counts $2856 down, showing frame $A2 near the end; at 0 it becomes behaviour $20 with frame $A3 and puts two copies of itself into objects 14 and 15 (behaviours $1E and $22), so it splits three ways, with sound $0D on voice 1.

Behaviour $32, the upper half of a figure two objects tall, a boss; its lower half is the next slot, rebuilt at the end of every pass by $EC46. While it is on screen it keeps $28A4 set, so no door can be used. It counts its record's +$0D down: above $15 it shows frame $F5 and, when slot 0 is free, fires into it (22 lines lower, behaviour $1C, frame $A4, sound $0F); below, frame $EF. When the count runs out it moves sideways 3 or 4 pixels a pass by its record's +$0B and hops along the arc at $283C (frames $F1, $F3), then picks a new direction and count at random (counts up to $1F, or $7F on stages $10, $16 and $1C). On stages $16 and $1C a hop's end also puts a second object in slot 1 (frame $A1, behaviour $1C) and sets $2856 to $3C.
Rebuilds the boss's lower half in the next slot: its frame plus 1, the same x, 21 lines lower, behaviour $34 and the same record number.
The NMI vector's handler: RTI, so the RESTORE key does nothing.

The game's start-up, run once after the title program hands over: the stack, $01=$35 (RAM everywhere but the I/O), the sound reset ($F889), all sprites on and multicolour, CIA interrupts off, the IRQ vector at $E1AC and the NMI at $EC65 ($FFFE and $FFFA, with $0314 too), the clock set to 5:00, the checkpoint (camera $001C/$019B, player x $22, line $30, colour 6), stage 0, the video modes and VIC bank 1 ($4000-$7FFF); then loads the overlay and the stage ($1B0D, $1B28), draws the screen ($13C6), zeroes the score, sets 25 magazines ($F359), full energy ($40) and 3 lives, draws the panel's score, and enters the main loop.

The wipe between stages: blanks the border and ANDs the character set at $4800-$4FFF with eight masks at a time, from $E99E or $E9DE by the stage, stepping through the masks eight times so the picture breaks up and disappears.
Operand of the AND at $EDC8, written by $ED6E with the first mask's address and moved on 8 a step.
The high byte of the operand of the AND at $EDC8, rewritten by $ED71, $EE21 before it runs.
The low byte of the operand of the AND at $EDD0, rewritten by $ED78, $EE2A before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the AND at $EDD0, rewritten by $ED7B, $EE32 before it runs.
The low byte of the operand of the AND at $EDD8, rewritten by $ED82, $EE3B before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the AND at $EDD8, rewritten by $ED85, $EE43 before it runs.
Inside $ED5A, where the second pair of mask reads begins. The loader's JSR $EDDD at $0555 is a call to the KERNAL's CIOUT, with the ROM banked in at that moment: it does not reach this code.
The low byte of the operand of the AND at $EDE0, rewritten by $ED8C, $EE4C before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the AND at $EDE0, rewritten by $ED8F, $EE54 before it runs.
The low byte of the operand of the AND at $EDE8, rewritten by $ED96, $EE5D before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the AND at $EDE8, rewritten by $ED99, $EE65 before it runs.
The low byte of the operand of the AND at $EDF0, rewritten by $EDA0, $EE6E before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the AND at $EDF0, rewritten by $EDA3, $EE76 before it runs.
The low byte of the operand of the AND at $EDF8, rewritten by $EDAA, $EE7F before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the AND at $EDF8, rewritten by $EDAD, $EE87 before it runs.
Inside $ED5A. The loader's JSR $EDFE is the KERNAL's UNLSN, made with the ROM banked in.
The low byte of the operand of the AND at $EE00, rewritten by $EDB4, $EE90 before it runs.
The high byte of the operand of the AND at $EE00, rewritten by $EDB7, $EE98 before it runs.
Inside $ED5A: steps the eight mask operands on 8 bytes. The loader's JSR $EE13 is the KERNAL's ACPTR, made with the ROM banked in.

After a flip: colours the rightmost column (39) of the shown screen's 18 rows from the characters there, through the level's colour table at $FD9D, into colour RAM. Reads the screen at $4400 when $40 is set ($EF4C).
$EEA2 for the screen at $4400.
After a flip: colours the leftmost column (0) of the shown screen's 18 rows from the characters there, through $FD9D. Reads the screen at $4400 when $40 is set ($F099).
$EFEF for the screen at $4400.
After a flip: colours the top row's 40 characters from the shown screen ($4000, or $4400 when $40 is set) through $FD9D.
After a flip: colours the bottom row (17) of the shown screen through $FD9D.
Draws the six-digit score in $F356-$F358 (decimal) on the panel, each digit three characters tall: $33+digit, $3D+digit and $47+digit in rows at $42FC, $4324 and $434C.
Points for each score event, low two digits then middle two, read by $F20C with X even: 0 gives 400, 2 200, 4 300, 6 1000, 8 5000.
The middle two digits of each entry of $F202.
Adds the points of entry X of $F202 to the score in decimal and redraws it.
A pseudo-random byte in A, kept across calls in $F26F-$F273 (shifting and mixing five bytes); keeps X and Y.
The random generator's five bytes of state, $F26F-$F273; A returns $F26F.
The random generator's second byte.
The random generator's third byte.
The random generator's fourth byte.
The random generator's fifth byte, which also takes the carry.
Waits until the raster is between lines $A4 and $B1, which paces the main loop to the frame.

Sorts the list of objects at $7F-$8E by line ($DF+n) with an insertion sort, so the multiplexer can place them top to bottom; then checks the player against them ($1018), finds the first object in use and sets the first sprite interrupt 13 lines above it ($F313) and the stop line $44.
The line of the first sprite interrupt, set by $F2B3 and written to $D012 by $136F.
Reads both joystick ports at once ($DC00 AND $DC01, so either port works) into $F355: up $08, down $04, left $02, right $01, fire $10. Left sets the facing $5C to 8 and right to 0.
The joystick as $F314 read it this pass.
The score, six decimal digits in $F356 (highest) to $F358.
The score's middle two digits.
The score's lowest two digits.

The spare magazines, two decimal digits shown beside the bullet icon: 25 at the start, one more every five seconds of the clock ($F47A) and one for each ammunition pickup; a magazine is used each time the gun's six rounds run out.
Draws the two digits of $F359 on the panel at $4317 and $4318 (characters $1B and up).
The player's energy, $40 when full: 10 off for a hazard, $10 back for an energy pickup.

Draws the energy bar on the panel from column $0E of the row at $4348: a full character $2B for each 8 points, then character 2 for the part, whose eight rows it rewrites at $5010-$5017 with the pattern from $3734 for the points left over, then blanks to column $18.
Draws the lives on the panel, character $29 for each of up to four, from column $0E of the row at $42F8, and blanks the rest to column $12.
The clock: $F421 counts passes from $3B down to a second, $F422 the seconds (decimal) and $F423 the minutes.
The clock's seconds, two decimal digits.
The clock's minutes.

Ticks the clock once a pass and draws it on the panel ($430B-$430E, with a colon $2A at $430C). Each second whose last digit is 0 or 5 adds a magazine. At 0:00 the player loses a life ($1974) and the clock is set to 9:00 for the next one.

No lives left. Shows GAME OVER on the panel, waits for fire, then 255 frames, then, while continues are left ($2865: two in a game), shows CONTINUE with a countdown from 9, about a second a digit: fire continues (clock back to 5:00, energy full, 25 magazines, the panel redrawn), and when the countdown or the continues run out it returns to the title ($0766). The KERNAL's LOAD name the export gave this address is wrong here: the KERNAL is banked out and this is the game's own code.
Returns 3. The loader's JSR $F5D2 at $0533 is made with the KERNAL banked in, where it reaches the ROM's code, not this.

Unpacks a file from ($64) to ($66). After an 18-byte header (byte $11 the number of blocks), each block reads three Huffman code tables ($F7D9: literal lengths built at $4000, match offsets at $4080, match lengths at $4100) and a 16-bit count of sequences, then repeats: a run of literal bytes copied from the input, then a copy from earlier output, offset and length decoded with the tables. Bits come from $F777.
Decodes one value with the code table at ($6F): reads bits until a code in the table matches, then reads the extra bits that value says and returns it in $6B/$6C.
The bit values 1, 2, 4 ... $80, used by $F719.
Moves A into X and reads that many bits ($F777).
Takes X bits from the bit buffer $71-$74 into $6B/$6C, refilling it two bytes at a time from the input at ($64).
Masks for 0-16 bits, low bytes: 0, 1, 3, 7 ... $FF.
Masks for 0-16 bits, high bytes.

Reads a Huffman table from the packed stream: a 5-bit count of code lengths, 4 bits each into $4180, then builds the codes in order of length into the table at ($6F), with each code's value $3C bytes further on.
Keeps X while $EA16 and $EAD4 call the sound.
Keeps Y while they call it.
Keeps A while they call it.
Jumps to $FA24, which silences all three voices, clears the SID and sets the volume to 15.
Jumps to $F95A: starts sound effect X on voice Y.

The sound effects' update, once a frame from the panel interrupt ($132B): for each voice that is playing, slides its frequency by the effect's step ($FA65/$FA68) and, when its time runs out, reads the effect's next command ($F8CA).

Reads a voice's next commands from its effect: $FF ends it (or starts it again when it loops), $FC stops the slide, $FD sets a new slide, $FE sets the pulse width; anything else is a waveform byte followed by the frequency (high, low), and the next step's length.

Starts effect X on voice Y: from the effect's address ($FA71/$FA83) takes its length (and the loop flag in bit 7), the slide, attack/decay, sustain/release, pulse width, the filter (when its low four bits are not 0 or 2: the mode and volume and the cutoff, and routes the voice through it) and the first waveform and frequency.
Silences the sound: clears each voice's state and the 25 SID registers, filter routing off, volume 15.
The register offset of each voice: 0, 7, 14.
Each voice's bit in the filter routing: 1, 2, 4.
The same bits inverted, to take a voice out of the filter.
The effect each voice is playing.
Each voice's place in its effect (0 when silent).
Each voice's time left on its present step.
Each voice's place to go back to when its effect loops.
Each voice's loop flag.
Each voice's frequency, low byte.
Each voice's frequency, high byte.
Each voice's frequency slide, low byte.
Each voice's frequency slide, high byte.
The voice's register offset while an effect is started or read.
The voice's filter bit while an effect is started.
The voice number while an effect is started.
Where the loop of the effect being started begins.
The voice's inverted filter bit while an effect is started.
The filter routing and resonance byte written to $D417.
The low bytes of the 18 sound effects' addresses ($FA95 to $FC80).
The high bytes of the 18 effects' addresses.

The 18 sound effects, numbered 0-$11 by their place in $FA71/$FA83: each a header (length and loop flag, slide, attack/decay, sustain/release, pulse, filter, waveform and frequency) and then commands for $F8CA. The calls to $F88C say which event plays which.

The stage's character properties, one byte for each of the 256 characters, copied from COL0 by $1B28: bit 7 solid floor, bit 6 ladder, bit 5 wall, bit 1 door, and bit 0 a character that holds the player (it sets $2411).
The byte between the property table and the colours: not loaded by either, not read.

The stage's .ATT file: three bytes, then the border and three background colours ($FD99-$FD9C, set by $136F every frame), then the colour of each of the 256 characters ($FD9D) for colour RAM, multicolour bit included.
The border colour, from the .ATT file.
Background colour 0.
Background colour 1 (multicolour).
Background colour 2 (multicolour).
The colour-RAM value of each of the stage's 256 characters, from the .ATT file: the low four bits the colour, bit 3 the multicolour switch.

Three bytes for each enemy record, built by $1B28 from the records' bytes $11, 6 and 4 (hit points, type and frame) and copied back into the records when a life starts ($19FA), so every enemy comes back whole. The list ends at the address in $1DA5/$1DA6.

Named only as the base of the reads $FF8F,X at $1050, $1061, $1F6A and $1F7B, which with X from $F0 wrap past $FFFF to the sort list at $7F-$8E. The bytes here are RAM the game never writes, the emulator's power-on pattern.
The character chosen at the title: 1 Riggs, 0 Murtaugh. Picks the player's sprites, colour, jump and push.
